extracted.intended_audience: administrative law scholars, practitioners, judges, and law students interested in notice-and-comment rulemaking and judicial review
extracted.subtask_description: A doctrinal and normative analysis arguing that Vermont Yankee forbids courts from imposing trial-like or other extra-statutory procedures on agency rulemaking, and that several modern administrative-law doctrines (ex parte prohibitions, anti-prejudgment rules, expanded notice requirements) conflict with that holding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on courts imposing extra-procedural requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court chastised the D.C. Circuit for forcing the NRC to employ procedures such as discovery and cross-examination in a notice-and-comment rulemaking when no organic statute, regulation, or constitutional provision required it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vermont Yankee stands for the principle that courts should not require agencies to use procedures beyond those mandated by the agency's organic statute, applicable regulations, or the Constitution. The article treats this as the central holding whose 'natural reading' limits lower-court interference with agency procedural choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery and cross-examination not required absent statutory authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery and cross-examination are not required in notice-and-comment rulemaking unless an organic statute, regulation, or constitutional provision mandates them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trial-like procedures (e.g., discovery, cross-examination) are inappropriate add-ons imposed by courts in rulemaking contexts; agencies should not be compelled to adopt them through judicial fiat. The authors argue prior doctrinal developments that effectively require such procedures conflict with Vermont Yankee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on lower-court interference with agency discretion and autonomy
rubrics_metrics.description: Vermont Yankee is an important decision restraining lower courts from unduly interfering with agency discretion and autonomy by imposing additional procedural demands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should defer to agencies' statutory procedural frameworks; interventions that substitute judicial procedural preferences for those chosen by the agency or Congress are improper. The article uses this as a baseline principle for evaluating other doctrines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of ex parte contact prohibitions in rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine prohibiting agency ex parte contacts in rulemakings is, the authors contend, inconsistent with the proper reading of Vermont Yankee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece argues that regulatory rules barring ex parte contacts operate as judicially or administratively imposed procedural constraints that go beyond statutory requirements and therefore should be reexamined or rejected under Vermont Yankee's principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of anti-prejudgment doctrine in rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine forbidding agency 'prejudgment' in rulemakings conflicts with Vermont Yankee's holding and underlying policies, according to the authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules that prevent agencies from forming preliminary views or seeking input that might appear like 'prejudgment' are viewed as judicially-created limits on agency procedure; the authors argue such doctrines improperly constrain agencies and should be reconsidered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Challenge to modern expansive views of APA notice requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Mainstream applications of the APA's notice requirements — i.e., modern, expanded conceptions of what notice must contain or how it must be conducted — violate the holding of Vermont Yankee as properly understood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When courts interpret the APA's notice-and-comment requirements in ways that effectively force agencies to adopt more elaborate or trial-like procedures than the statute requires, they are imposing extra-statutory procedural burdens contrary to Vermont Yankee. The authors examine these mainstream applications and argue for retraction or limitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural reading of Vermont Yankee as a limiting doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'natural reading' of Vermont Yankee supports rejecting doctrines that impose additional procedural constraints on rulemaking (ex parte rules, anti-prejudgment rules, and expanded notice requirements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article frames an interpretive approach — the 'natural reading' — that emphasizes Vermont Yankee's text and rationale as limiting tools for judges assessing whether other procedural doctrines are compatible with the Supreme Court's restraint on imposing procedures in rulemaking.
